3567.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂éd
Unadapted borrowing from Italian a vista (“at sight, on presentation”). The first element, a (“at, to, in”), is from Latin ad (“to, toward; at”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“toward, to, at”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). The second element, vista (“sight, view”), is a deverbal noun related to vedere (“to see”), from Latin videō (“to see, perceive”), from Proto-Italic *widēō (“to see”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *weyd- (“to see, know”). First attested in 1878.
Compare the parallel borrowings Norwegian Nynorsk a vista, Danish a vista, Swedish a vist

107247.etyen:
Borrowed from Late Latin abracadabra (“magic formula”). The Late Latin word is of uncertain ultimate origin. It is attested in Serenus Sammonicus's medical poem Liber Medicinalis around the beginning of the 3rd century CE, where it is prescribed as a charm against fever: the word is written repeatedly with one letter removed on each successive line until it forms a narrowing triangle or cone. Proposed connections with the Gnostic name ἀβράξας (abráxas, “Abraxas”) and with various Aramaic or Hebrew expressions remain uncertain and are not securely established.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk abrakada

30959.etyen:
The verb is inherited from Old Norse koma (“to come”), from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to come, go”). The noun is a substantivization of the verb.
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk koma and komme, Danish komme, Swedish komma, Icelandic koma, Faroese koma, English come, West Frisian komme, Dutch komen, German kommen and Gothic 𐌵𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (qiman, “to come”). More distantly, compare Latin veniō (“I come”) and Ancient Greek βαίνω (baínō, “I walk, go”).

1004527.etyen:
Literally “Swedish conditions”, from svenske (“Swedish”) + tilstander (“conditions, states”).
The expression has been used in Norwegian media since at least the 1960s with varying reference to Sweden or Swedish society. In the 2010s, especially during the 2017 Norwegian election campaign, it became established as a political expression in debates about immigration, integration, and crime.
Compare det svenska tillståndet (“the Swedish condition, the Swedish state of affairs”), borrowed from the Norwegian expression.
